> > What is an RSA that you mentioned?
>
> RSA = **Responsive Search Ad**.
>
> It’s the standard Google Search ad format where you give Google multiple:
>
> ```text
> headlines
> descriptions
> ```
>
> Then Google mixes and matches them to create different ad versions depending on the search.
>
> For example, for `Company Logo Shirts`, you might give Google headlines like:
>
> ```text
> Company Logo Shirts
> Business Logo Shirts
> No Minimum Logo Shirts
> Fast Local Turnaround
> Upload Your Logo
> ```
>
> And descriptions like:
>
> ```text
> Custom logo shirts for small teams and businesses. No minimum order required.
> Upload your logo for fast local printing near St. Louis and St. Charles.
> ```
>
> Google then tests combinations automatically.
>
> When I said “pin,” I meant you can force certain headlines into certain positions. For example, pinning `Company Logo Shirts` to Headline 1 makes sure the ad always starts with that core intent. But too much pinning limits Google’s testing, so I’d only lightly pin H1 for this ad group.

> **Why `Trades & Crew Shirts` May Deserve Its Own Ad Group**
>
> Trade businesses buy shirts often and usually have clear commercial intent:
>
> ```text
> plumbing company shirts
> electrician shirts
> hvac shirts
> landscaping company shirts
> construction shirts
> contractor work shirts
> work shirts with logo
> crew shirts with logo
> ```
>
> That is different from:
>
> ```text
> staff shirts
> employee shirts
> restaurant staff shirts
> office staff shirts
> uniform shirts
> ```
>
> The ad copy would also be different. Trades care about looking professional, crew identity, durable workwear, visibility, fast reorders, and logos. Staff shirts care more about employees, shops, restaurants, events, and small teams.

> > So does it really make a difference? I guess I've never fully experienced the feeling of the "higher intent customers" what even measures that? When we're paying more for a bid, is it like ACTUALLY a higher quality click? Or are clicks just clicks?
>
> Clicks are not just clicks. But paying more **does not automatically** mean the click is higher quality.
>
> A higher bid mainly buys you more eligibility and better position in auctions. The quality comes from **which searches you’re willing to bid on**, not the bid itself.
>
> Example:
>
> ```text
> "staff tshirts" broad match
> ```
>
> That bought lots of clicks, but Google could match it loosely. Some people may have wanted staff shirt ideas, retail uniforms, employee shirt policies, big-box brand shirts, etc.
>
> Compare that to:
>
> ```text
> [company logo shirts]
> [custom work shirts with logo]
> [family vacation shirts]
> [shirt printing st louis]
> ```
>
> Those are higher intent because the person is closer to buying the exact thing you sell.
>
> **What Measures Higher Intent**
>
> Before conversion tracking is fixed, you measure it with proxies:
>
> ```text
> Search term relevance
> Click-to-call activity
> Quote form starts/submits
> Orders you can tie to ad timing
> Time on site / engaged sessions
> Pages viewed
> Messages or emails mentioning Google
> ```
>
> After tracking is fixed, you measure it properly:
>
> ```text
> Cost per call
> Cost per quote request
> Cost per order
> Conversion rate by keyword
> Search term to sale quality
> Revenue per lead/order
> ```
>
> **What A Higher CPC Cap Actually Does**
>
> If your cap is too low, Google may skip auctions for valuable searches like:
>
> ```text
> business shirts with logo
> custom work shirts with logo
> company logo shirts
> custom shirts st louis
> ```
>
> because competitors are bidding more.
>
> Raising the cap from `$1.71` to `$2.10` says:
>
> ```text
> I am willing to pay a little more when the search is relevant.
> ```
>
> It does **not** say:
>
> ```text
> I want Google to buy any click at $2.10.
> ```
>
> That’s why your keyword list and negatives matter so much.
>
> **Practical Example**
>
> A bad $1.20 click:
>
> ```text
> t shirt designer
> shirt maker
> family reunion shirt ideas
> ```
>
> A good $2.10 click:
>
> ```text
> custom work shirts with logo
> company logo shirts
> family vacation shirts
> shirt printing st louis
> ```
>
> The second click costs more, but it may be 5-10x more likely to become a call/order.
>
> **My Honest Take**
>
> For you right now, the “higher intent customer” feeling should look like fewer clicks but more people who:
>
> ```text
> call asking about an actual order
> upload a logo
> ask about pickup/turnaround
> request pricing for a group/team/business
> mention a specific event/date/order quantity
> ```
>
> If clicks dropped and orders/calls stayed similar, the cleanup worked.
>
> If clicks dropped and orders/calls also dropped, then we tightened too hard or bids are too low.
>
> That’s why I’d make a cautious bid change, not a big one:
>
> ```text
> $1.71 -> $2.10
> ```
>
> Then judge the search terms and real inquiries, not just click count.

> Yes, it is mostly Google tags/code, but it can be pretty simple.
>
> Think of it like this:
>
> ```text
> Google Ads conversion action = what you want to count
> Google tag / GTM = the tracking code on your site
> Trigger/event = when Google should count it
> ```
>
> For Print-MO, I’d set up tracking in this order:
>
> **1. Calls From Ads**
> This tracks people who tap the call button/call asset directly from your Google ad.
>
> No website code needed if it’s call asset tracking.
>
> Track as primary:
>
> ```text
> Phone call lead
> Count: One
> Minimum call length: 60 seconds if available
> ```
>
> **2. Quote Form Submitted**
> Best version: after someone submits a quote/contact form, send them to a thank-you page like:
>
> ```text
> /thank-you
> /quote-submitted
> ```
>
> Then Google counts a conversion when that page loads.
>
> This is usually easier and cleaner than tracking every button click.
>
> Track as primary:
>
> ```text
> Quote request
> Count: One
> ```
>
> **3. Website Click-To-Call**
> This tracks when someone clicks your phone number on the site.
>
> This does require code or Google Tag Manager. It tracks the click, not necessarily a completed phone call, but it’s still useful.
>
> Track as primary or secondary depending how much phone traffic you get.
>
> **4. Online Order Completed**
> If your site has checkout/order completion, track the final confirmation page or completed order event.
>
> Track as primary:
>
> ```text
> Purchase / Order complete
> Count: Every
> ```
>
> **5. Secondary Actions**
> These are useful, but don’t optimize around them first:
>
> ```text
> Logo upload
> Started design flow
> Contact page view
> Clicked “Get Quote”
> Engaged visit
> ```
>
> **Direct Code vs Google Tag Manager**
>
> Simplest long-term setup:
>
> ```text
> Install Google Tag Manager once
> Use GTM to add Google Ads conversion tags
> Set triggers for form submit, phone click, thank-you page, etc.
> ```
>
> Direct-code setup also works:
>
> ```text
> Add Google tag to every page
> Add event snippet to thank-you page or specific button clicks
> ```
>
> Google’s docs confirm this general setup: you create conversion actions, add the Google tag to the site, and add event snippets or click handlers for button/phone clicks. Phone call conversions can also be tracked from ads/call assets. Sources: [Google tag setup](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6331314), [conversion types](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/1722054), [phone call tracking](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6100664), [phone number click tracking](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6095878).

> Primary: Quote submitted
> Primary: Calls from ads
> Primary: Website click-to-call
> Primary: Online order complete, if checkout exists
> Secondary: Logo upload / design start
> ```

I continued the site inspection. You are not starting from zero.

Your live Shopify site already has:

```text
Google Ads ID: AW-16683308706
GA4 ID: G-5X1Z8CQDJE
GTM container: GTM-MKLTDSH2
```

What’s missing is the important part: I do **not** see clear Google Ads conversion tracking for quote submissions, website phone clicks, or the quote calculator. Your Shopify Google app appears to be handling ecommerce events like `purchase`, `begin_checkout`, `add_to_cart`, etc., but your lead actions are the bigger gap.

**What I Found**
Your landing-page quote widget already pushes lead-like events into `dataLayer`, including:

```text
quote_type_selected
quote_quantity_selected
generate_lead
```

Your quote page also has a real quote calculator form with:

```text
Calculate
Email Detailed Quote
```

Your contact page has a standard Shopify contact form.

Your phone links exist:

```text
tel:6367931975
tel:+6367931975
```

But I did not see phone conversion snippets or Google Ads lead conversion snippets firing in the page HTML.

**Best Setup**
I would do this:

1. Leave Shopify Google & YouTube app tracking alone for purchases.
   Do not duplicate purchase tracking manually.

2. In Google Ads, create these conversion actions:

```text
PM - Quote Lead
PM - Calls From Ads
PM - Website Phone Click
PM - Purchase
```

3. Set these as primary:

```text
PM - Quote Lead
PM - Calls From Ads
PM - Purchase, if online checkout orders matter
```

4. Set this as secondary at first:

```text
PM - Website Phone Click
```

Reason: phone click only proves they tapped the number, not that a real call happened.

5. In GTM, add one unified custom event for lead form submits, something like:

```text
pm_lead_submit
```

That should fire on:

```text
Landing page quote form
Landing page question form
Get A Quote calculator form
Contact form
```

6. Then create a Google Ads Conversion Tracking tag in GTM that fires on:

```text
Custom Event = pm_lead_submit
```

7. Create another Google Ads tag or phone-click conversion trigger for:

```text
Click URL starts with tel:
```

**Important**
The most “foolproof” tracking would be a real thank-you page after every successful form submit. Your current setup does not clearly use one, so event tracking through GTM is the practical path.

Google’s own docs support this structure: use event snippets/GTM for button or form conversions, use phone tracking separately, and avoid duplicate Shopify purchase tags. Sources: [Google web conversions](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/16560108), [Google tag](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/7548399), [Shopify Google & YouTube app tracking](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/13494537), [phone call tracking](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6100664).

I would not touch bidding strategy again until this is tracking. Right now, this is the highest-leverage fix.

I can continue from the compacted state. The important finding is:

Your site already has the base tracking installed:

```text
Google Ads: AW-16683308706
GA4: G-5X1Z8CQDJE
GTM: GTM-MKLTDSH2
```

But the inspected pages do **not** show an explicit Google Ads conversion firing for leads:

```text
Quote page: no explicit Ads conversion event
Landing page: no explicit Ads conversion event
Contact page: no explicit Ads conversion event
Phone links exist: tel:6367931975 / tel:+6367931975
```

**Recommended Setup**
Do this in this order.

1. In Google Ads, create `PM - Quote Lead`

Settings:

```text
Goal/category: Submit lead form
Optimization: Primary
Count: One
Value: no value for now, or fixed value later
Attribution: Data-driven if available
Implementation: Google Tag Manager
```

Then Google Ads will give you:

```text
Conversion ID: 16683308706
Conversion Label: [unique label Google gives you]
```

2. In GTM, create a trigger:

```text
Trigger name: CE - pm_lead_submit
Trigger type: Custom Event
Event name: pm_lead_submit
```

This is the clean event we want to fire only after a real quote/contact submission.

3. In GTM, create the tag:

```text
Tag name: GAds - PM - Quote Lead
Tag type: Google Ads Conversion Tracking
Conversion ID: 16683308706
Conversion Label: from Google Ads
Trigger: CE - pm_lead_submit
```

4. For the most foolproof setup, add this event to the Shopify form success state, not just the button click:

```html
<script>
window.dataLayer = window.dataLayer || [];
window.dataLayer.push({
  event: 'pm_lead_submit',
  lead_form: 'quote_or_contact',
  page_path: window.location.pathname
});
</script>
```

This should fire after successful submit on:

```text
/pages/get-a-quote-1
/pages/contact
landing page quote/question form
```

A button-click trigger is easier, but it can overcount failed forms. The success-state event is the cleaner version.

5. Add `PM - Website Phone Click`

Google Ads settings:

```text
Goal/category: Phone call lead
Optimization: Secondary at first
Count: One
```

GTM trigger:

```text
Trigger type: Just Links
Click URL starts with tel:
```

GTM tag:

```text
Google Ads Conversion Tracking
Trigger: tel: click trigger
```

6. Add `PM - Calls From Ads`

This is for calls directly from your Google ad/call asset. It does not require website code.

Settings:

```text
Optimization: Primary
Minimum call length: 60 seconds if available
Count: One
```

7. Leave purchase tracking alone until verified.

**Primary vs Secondary**
Use this:

```text
Primary:
PM - Quote Lead
PM - Calls From Ads
PM - Purchase, only if confirmed not duplicated

Secondary:
PM - Website Phone Click
PM - Quote Intent / generate_lead
```

Your site already has `generate_lead`, `quote_type_selected`, and `quote_quantity_selected` events in the GTM/dataLayer world. I would not use those as the main conversion yet. They are useful intent signals, but a true quote/contact submit is what should count as the lead.

Sources used for the implementation path: [Google Ads conversions in GTM](https://support.google.com/tagmanager/answer/6105160), [track website clicks](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6331304), [phone click tracking](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6095878), [phone call tracking](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6100664).

**How It Connects**
The flow will be:

```text
User submits quote form
Your website pushes an event like pm_lead_submit into dataLayer

```

```text
When this custom form succeeds, fire this conversion.
```

`Conversion Linker` is not the conversion tracker. It only preserves the Google ad click ID so Google can connect the later lead back to the ad click.

